item.title: Listening to Claude Debussy – Nocturne (L. 82)
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: I was researching early Debussy, trying to understand how he got from where he started to where he ended up, and this piece appeared. The opening is slow and loose, almost like the pianist is...
item.content:encoded:
I was researching early Debussy, trying to understand how he got from where he started to where he ended up, and this piece appeared.

The opening is slow and loose, almost like the pianist is still deciding what to play. There’s no dramatic entry. It just begins, gently, and I found myself relaxing without noticing. The melody drifts more than it moves forward, and somehow that’s enough to hold my attention.

What I wasn’t prepared for was the middle section. Something shifts. The texture thickens, the dynamic rises, and the piece feels urgent. It surprised me. And then it passes. The calm returns, the melody comes back, and the piece closes as gently as it opened.

By the end I felt like I’d been let in on something private. Not a grand statement. Just a mood, carefully held.

item.title: Listening to Mykola Leontovych – Dudaryk
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: Analysing this piece provides a good contrast to the contemporary works I’ve examined. Performed by the O. Koshetz Choir, this a cappella choral piece demonstrates how the human voice alone can create a complex narrative structure...
item.content:encoded:
Analysing this piece provides a good contrast to the contemporary works I’ve examined. Performed by the O. Koshetz Choir, this a cappella choral piece demonstrates how the human voice alone can create a complex narrative structure and emotional arc.

The piece starts with a simple, rhythmic motive that mimics the sound of a piper’s pipe. This motive acts as a leitmotif, recurring throughout to maintain the connection to the titular character. The build-up is achieved through increasing rhythmic complexity and a broadening of the choral harmony, moving from a transparent, light texture to a much denser, more resonant one.

The piece feels like a celebration of folk life, yet it’s also grounded in intensity. The timbre of the choir shifts from playful and light in the initial verses to a powerful resonance in the climactic sections. The way the different vocal lines intertwine feels like a “reflective mosaic” of people coming together, each adding their own color to the collective whole.

It reminds me that even without external instruments or a dedicated narrator, the human voice can convey a powerful sense of story and emotion. This has given me much to think about in terms of how I might use choral elements or even just layered vocal textures in my own project.

item.title: Listening to Marcello – Concerto for oboe and strings Adagio in D minor
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: The opening dissonance of Marcello’s Oboe Concerto is one of the things I find most interesting. It creates a small moment of tension that does not seem to predict the beautiful melody that follows. This makes the...
item.content:encoded:
The opening dissonance of Marcello’s Oboe Concerto is one of the things I find most interesting. It creates a small moment of tension that does not seem to predict the beautiful melody that follows. This makes the entrance of the oboe feel even more expressive.

For me, the oboe sounds almost like a singer. Its melody moves up and down in a way that reminds me of someone crying or trying to express something difficult. This makes the piece feel very sad and emotional. The oboe has a very direct and human quality.

I also notice the repeated movement of the strings underneath the melody. They seem to be constantly moving forward, but slowly, almost like dragging their feet. This creates a dark and somber atmosphere that remains present through much of the piece. I find this interesting because the oboe melody itself is beautiful and lyrical, while the string accompaniment is more repetitive and restrained.

This contrast between the expressive melody and the repetitive background is, for me, one of the strongest aspects of the piece. The strings create a continuous emotional environment while the oboe seems to speak or cry above it. The simplicity of the accompaniment gives the oboe space, allowing the melody to carry most of the emotional weight.

item.title: Listening to Arvo Pärt – Spiegel im Spiegel
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: I listened to Spiegel im Spiegel in versions for violin, viola, and cello. I preferred the cello version because I think its darker timbre creates a stronger contrast with the high and soft sound of the piano....
item.content:encoded:
I listened to Spiegel im Spiegel in versions for violin, viola, and cello. I preferred the cello version because I think its darker timbre creates a stronger contrast with the high and soft sound of the piano. The piece feels very solemn and simple. Although there is a piano, I hear the string instrument almost as the main character, while the piano creates a kind of musical landscape around it. It provides the harmonic space without taking the main focus.

At some moments, the piece reminds me of a lullaby. I particularly like the way Pärt uses the piano’s lower notes. They appear at carefully chosen moments and can create a feeling of arrival or ending. However, the higher piano notes continue, and the string instrument follows them. Because of this, the music never completely settles. There is always a sense of continuation.

This relates to Pärt’s style of using simplicity, repetition, and silence as important musical elements. I read the phrase “the composer who made silence sing”, and I can understand this idea in Spiegel im Spiegel. There is not complete silence in the piece, but a strong sense of quietness is always present. The spaces between the notes become almost as important as the notes themselves.
